abstracts.abstract: This paper introduces a novel theoretical framework reconceptualizing human-robot collaboration as a dynamic co-adaptation process rather than a unidirectional instruction-following paradigm. Current models in human-robot interaction (HRI) predominantly frame collaboration through static role assignments, failing to capture the bidirectional temporal evolution of joint activities. Drawing upon distributed cognition theory and ecological psychology, we propose the Collaborative Adaptive Systems (CAS) framework, which conceptualizes human-robot collaboration as emergent behavior arising from mutual adjustments between partners operating within shared perceptual fields. Our theoretical analysis identifies three critical dimensions of co-adaptation: predictive alignment, corrective synchronization, and anticipatory coordination. We validate the framework's explanatory power by applying it to existing literature on human-robot communication in multi-task scenarios, demonstrating its capacity to resolve apparent contradictions in findings regarding robot autonomy levels and user preferences. The CAS framework fundamentally shifts how researchers conceptualize the relationship between human factors and autonomous systems, offering new design principles for social robots that emphasize adaptive capacity over fixed behavioral repertoires. This paradigm innovation provides a unifying theoretical foundation for understanding how mutual predictability develops in HRI contexts, with significant implications for robot design and evaluation methodologies.

Accurate prediction of human trust dynamics in human-robot interaction remains a critical challenge for effective autonomous systems deployment. Existing trust calibration models rely predominantly on performance-based metrics, neglecting the multidimensional nature of trust formation in social contexts. This paper presents an enhanced integrative model of trust dynamics that substantially improves upon current theoretical approaches by incorporating emotional attunement, perceived intent, and contextual risk assessment as primary determinants of trust evolution. We conducted a meta-analysis of 47 empirical studies in HRI evaluation contexts, encompassing 2,340 participants, to validate model parameters and identify boundary conditions. Results demonstrate that the enhanced model explains 34% more variance in trust-related behavioral outcomes compared to existing performance-only models. Structural equation modeling revealed that perceived robot benevolence operates as a proximal trust antecedent, while technical competence functions as a threshold condition rather than a primary driver. Furthermore, we identify significant moderating effects of user prior experience with technology and task criticality. These findings yield improved design guidelines for assistive robotics applications where appropriate trust calibration directly impacts user safety and acceptance. The proposed model provides human factors researchers with a more complete theoretical tool for predicting and engineering trust in human-robot interaction scenarios.

This paper presents RoboMorph, a fundamentally redesigned architecture for social robots that challenges the prevailing anthropomorphic paradigm in robot design. Current social robot platforms predominantly mimic human physical characteristics, often creating uncanny interactions and unrealistic user expectations. RoboMorph introduces a novel adaptive morphology system featuring modular external structure with variable rigidity and shape memory materials, enabling real-time physical reconfiguration based on interaction context and user needs. The system incorporates a hierarchical perception-action architecture that prioritizes functional demonstration over humanoid appearance. We developed a comprehensive user study with 120 participants comparing RoboMorph against three established social robot platforms across domestic assistance, therapeutic, and collaborative work scenarios. Results indicate that participants rated RoboMorph as significantly more trustworthy and competent, while reporting lower anxiety levels despite its non-anthropomorphic appearance. Critically, the adaptive morphology enabled RoboMorph to transition seamlessly between configurations suited for different tasks, demonstrating superior versatility in human-robot collaboration contexts. The robot's ability to physically manifest appropriate form for each interaction type represents a paradigm innovation in HRI, shifting design focus from appearance-based social cues toward functionally-responsive physical adaptation. This work establishes new design principles for autonomous systems prioritizing interactional effectiveness over visual anthropomorphism.

Teleoperation of robotic systems in complex environments imposes substantial cognitive demands on operators, frequently resulting in fatigue, error, and reduced operational effectiveness. Current teleoperation interfaces in industrial robotics and assistive applications typically employ rigid visual feedback paradigms that fail to adapt to operator cognitive states and task demands. This paper presents AdaptHUD, an augmented cognitive support system that substantially improves teleoperation effectiveness through dynamic adaptation of information presentation based on real-time operator workload assessment. The system integrates physiological sensing (electrodermal activity, pupillometry, and heart rate variability) with performance metrics to construct a comprehensive cognitive load model. AdaptHUD dynamically adjusts visual augmentation density, haptic feedback intensity, and autonomy levels of the remote system based on detected operator states. We conducted a controlled evaluation with 36 professional operators performing simulated remote manipulation tasks of varying complexity. Results demonstrate significant improvements: 28% reduction in task completion time, 41% decrease in error rates, and 52% reduction in subjective workload compared to conventional fixed-interface teleoperation. Critically, the system maintained effectiveness across diverse user populations with varying experience levels, indicating robust transferability. This contribution advances the state-of-the-art in human-robot interaction for teleoperation applications, providing a practical framework for adaptive interfaces that optimize human-robot communication under varying operational conditions.
